title: "Reading topic-model output carefully"
subtitle: "Topic counts, LDA fitting, and random starts"
description: "Learn how LDA groups co-occurring words, how diagnostics inform the topic count, and why no single metric chooses k for you."
categories: [signals and discovery, topic modeling, inaugural addresses]

Priya receives five numbered topics and a request to name them before lunch. Each table row contains a few common words and a number.

The table can encourage interpretations that exceed the evidence. A topic model produces topics even when those topics vary across fits. The analyst must compare results from different random starts.

::: {.callout-tip}
## What you will learn

This lesson shows how to:

- explain Latent Dirichlet Allocation in everyday language.
- build a paragraph-level document-feature matrix.
- compare candidate topic counts with three diagnostics.
- distinguish an LDA model from the algorithm used to fit it.
- fit a five-topic LDA model with explicit seeds.
- match topics across runs by their top terms.
- compare observed agreement with a random-label null.
:::

```{r}
#| include: false

options(warn = 2)
stopifnot(identical(getOption("warn"), 2L))
```

## Build the matrix

**Latent Dirichlet Allocation**, usually shortened to **LDA**, groups words that tend to appear in the same documents. Here each document is one paragraph. A **document-feature matrix** stores document rows and word columns. The value `k` is the number of topics the analyst asks the model to find.

```{r}
library(dplyr)
library(tibble)
library(stringr)
library(purrr)
library(readr)
library(quanteda)
library(topicmodels)

source("R/inaugural-corpus.R")
source("R/permutation-null.R")

paragraphs <- inaugural_paragraphs()

paragraph_tokens <- tokens(
  paragraphs$paragraph,
  remove_punct = TRUE,
  remove_numbers = TRUE
) |>
  tokens_tolower() |>
  tokens_remove(stopwords("en"))

paragraph_dfm <- dfm(paragraph_tokens)
trimmed_dfm <- dfm_trim(paragraph_dfm, min_termfreq = 5)
lda_input <- convert(trimmed_dfm, to = "topicmodels")

matrix_summary <- tibble(
  measure = c("documents", "features", "nonzero term counts"),
  value = c(ndoc(trimmed_dfm), nfeat(trimmed_dfm), sum(trimmed_dfm))
)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(
  matrix_summary,
  col.names = c("Measure", "Value"),
  caption = "The trimmed paragraph matrix for LDA",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  identical(nrow(paragraphs), 1377L),
  identical(ndoc(trimmed_dfm), 1377L),
  identical(nfeat(trimmed_dfm), 2587L),
  identical(sum(trimmed_dfm), 52934),
  identical(nrow(lda_input), 1377L),
  identical(ncol(lda_input), 2587L)
)
```

Trimming keeps words that appear at least five times in the paragraph corpus.
The matrix has 1,377 paragraph documents and 2,587 word features.

Paragraphs give the model 1,377 documents instead of 60 whole speeches. Each
document contains fewer words, so the model calculates an estimate of its topic mixture from
less evidence. Document size is therefore part of model design. This modest
corpus describes these speeches rather than political language generally.

## Compare candidate topic counts

There is no single correct value of `k`. Fewer topics create broad groups.
More topics divide the same vocabulary into smaller groups. The appropriate
value depends on the planned analysis.

The committed diagnostic study fits `k = 3` through `k = 8` under three random
starts. It builds the vocabulary from training speeches and evaluates
perplexity on held-out speeches. Three measures ask different questions:

- **Held-out perplexity** measures how poorly the fitted model predicts word
  counts in held-out speeches. Lower is better.
- **Semantic coherence** asks whether a topic's most probable words appear
  together in the training paragraphs. Higher values, which are less negative
  here, are better.
- **Adjusted top-word exclusivity** measures whether those words concentrate in
  one topic rather than occur across all topics. Higher is better. The
  adjustment removes the \(1/k\) share expected under equal distribution.

```{r}
topic_diagnostics <- read_csv(
  "data/inaugural/topic-k-diagnostics.csv",
  na = character(),
  col_types = cols(
    k = col_integer(),
    seeds = col_integer(),
    coherence_mean = col_double(),
    coherence_low = col_double(),
    coherence_high = col_double(),
    exclusivity_mean = col_double(),
    exclusivity_low = col_double(),
    exclusivity_high = col_double(),
    perplexity_mean = col_double(),
    perplexity_low = col_double(),
    perplexity_high = col_double(),
    coherence_rank = col_integer(),
    exclusivity_rank = col_integer(),
    perplexity_rank = col_integer(),
    selected = col_logical(),
    selection_reason = col_character()
  )
)

diagnostic_display <- topic_diagnostics |>
  transmute(
    k,
    coherence = round(coherence_mean, 3),
    coherence_rank,
    adjusted_exclusivity = round(exclusivity_mean, 3),
    exclusivity_rank,
    heldout_perplexity = round(perplexity_mean, 1),
    perplexity_rank,
    used_below = if_else(selected, "yes", "no")
  )

selected_diagnostics <- topic_diagnostics |>
  filter(selected)

three_topic_diagnostics <- topic_diagnostics |>
  filter(k == 3L)

coherence_lead <- (
  selected_diagnostics$coherence_mean -
    three_topic_diagnostics$coherence_mean
)
selected_coherence_spread <- (
  selected_diagnostics$coherence_high -
    selected_diagnostics$coherence_low
)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(
  diagnostic_display,
  col.names = c(
    "k",
    "Coherence",
    "Coherence rank",
    "Adjusted exclusivity",
    "Exclusivity rank",
    "Held-out perplexity",
    "Perplexity rank",
    "Used below"
  ),
  caption = "Three diagnostics give different preferred topic counts",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  identical(topic_diagnostics$k, 3:8),
  all(topic_diagnostics$seeds == 3L),
  identical(
    topic_diagnostics$k[
      topic_diagnostics$coherence_rank == 1L
    ],
    5L
  ),
  identical(
    topic_diagnostics$k[
      topic_diagnostics$exclusivity_rank == 1L
    ],
    3L
  ),
  identical(
    topic_diagnostics$k[
      topic_diagnostics$perplexity_rank == 1L
    ],
    3L
  ),
  identical(selected_diagnostics$k, 5L),
  identical(
    round(selected_diagnostics$coherence_mean, 3),
    -1.603
  ),
  identical(round(coherence_lead, 3), 0.020),
  identical(round(selected_coherence_spread, 3), 0.095)
)
```

The diagnostics do not agree. Three topics have the best held-out perplexity
and adjusted exclusivity. Five topics have the best mean coherence. This lesson
uses five because it gives coherence priority for this teaching example. Three
would also be a defensible choice if prediction or top-word concentration
mattered more. The later seed check examines only `k = 5`, so it cannot choose
between five and three.

The coherence lead over three topics is only
`r round(coherence_lead, 3)`, while the three five-topic starts span
`r round(selected_coherence_spread, 3)`. Rank 1 does not establish a clear advantage here.
These ranges come from three starts on one speech-grouped split, not confidence
intervals or a validated optimum for another corpus.

Do not choose `k` because its word table is easiest to name. That choice uses
the output to select the model retrospectively. Set the diagnostics and their
priority before reading topic tables. Then read the topics. People must examine
the results because predictive fit and automated coherence do not
guarantee useful or understandable topics.

::: {.callout-note}
## The model and fitting method are separate choices

The topicmodels package can fit LDA in two ways. **Variational expectation
maximization**, or **VEM**, approximates the model's probability distributions.
This lesson uses VEM. **Gibbs sampling** draws samples from those distributions
across successive iterations. The analyst chooses the iteration count,
warm-up, and number of retained samples. Both methods fit LDA but can return
different answers.

Other topic models use different assumptions. LDA cannot represent a tendency
for some topics to appear together in the same documents. A correlated topic
model can represent that tendency.
A structural topic model can use document information such as year to calculate
estimates of topic prevalence or content. Seeded and supervised topic models add analyst
guidance or an outcome. These models answer different questions and are not
necessary for every analysis.
:::

## Fit five topics three times

The analyst chooses `k = 5`. The seed in `control = list(seed = ...)` fixes the
random starting values used by the LDA fitting algorithm. It does not choose
`k`, and it does not prove that the fitted topics are the only possible
solution.

The committed diagnostic study used training and held-out speeches to inform
that choice. The three objects below are new full-corpus fits for inspection
at the selected resolution. They are not the diagnostic models.

```{r}
top_terms <- function(model, n = 10L) {
  beta <- posterior(model)$terms
  bind_rows(lapply(seq_len(nrow(beta)), function(topic) {
    ordered <- sort(beta[topic, ], decreasing = TRUE)
    tibble(
      topic = topic,
      term = names(ordered)[seq_len(n)],
      beta = as.numeric(ordered[seq_len(n)])
    )
  }))
}

set.seed(42)
lda_a <- LDA(
  lda_input,
  k = 5,
  method = "VEM",
  control = list(seed = 42)
)

set.seed(7)
lda_b <- LDA(
  lda_input,
  k = 5,
  method = "VEM",
  control = list(seed = 7)
)

set.seed(2024)
lda_c <- LDA(
  lda_input,
  k = 5,
  method = "VEM",
  control = list(seed = 2024)
)

terms_a <- top_terms(lda_a, n = 10L)
terms_b <- top_terms(lda_b, n = 10L)
terms_c <- top_terms(lda_c, n = 10L)

topics_a <- terms_a |>
  slice_head(n = 8, by = topic) |>
  summarise(top_terms = paste(term, collapse = ", "), .by = topic)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(
  topics_a,
  col.names = c("Topic number", "Top terms"),
  caption = "Top terms from a five-topic LDA model with seed 42",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  identical(nrow(topics_a), 5L),
  identical(
    topics_a$top_terms[1],
    "country, power, can, us, must, government, people, new"
  ),
  identical(
    terms_a$term[terms_a$topic == 5][1:3],
    c("must", "government", "people")
  )
)
```

The row names identify topics by number. The words are high-probability terms under this fitted model, not validated descriptions of a subject.

## Match topics across random starts

Topic numbers are arbitrary. Topic 1 in one run does not have to be topic 1 in another run. The comparison below matches topics by the largest total overlap in their top-10 term sets.

A **permutation null** computes the comparison again after shuffling topic assignments across top-term rows. The **p-value** adds 1 to the number of shuffled runs that match or exceed the observed overlap. It then divides that sum by the number of shuffled runs plus 1.

```{r}
permutations <- function(x) {
  if (length(x) == 1L) {
    return(list(x))
  }

  seq_along(x) |>
    map(\(i) {
      permutations(x[-i]) |>
        map(\(p) c(x[i], p))
    }) |>
    list_flatten()
}

best_topic_match <- function(terms_first, terms_second) {
  topics <- sort(unique(terms_first$topic))
  first_sets <- topics |>
    map(\(topic_id) terms_first$term[terms_first$topic == topic_id])
  second_sets <- topics |>
    map(\(topic_id) terms_second$term[terms_second$topic == topic_id])

  candidate_orders <- permutations(seq_along(topics))
  candidate_scores <- candidate_orders |>
    map_int(\(order) {
      seq_along(topics) |>
        map_int(\(i) length(intersect(first_sets[[i]], second_sets[[order[i]]]))) |>
        sum()
    })

  best_order <- candidate_orders[[which.max(candidate_scores)]]

  tibble(
    topic_first = topics,
    topic_second = topics[best_order],
    shared_top_10_terms = seq_along(topics) |>
      map_int(\(i) length(intersect(first_sets[[i]], second_sets[[best_order[i]]])))
  )
}

seed_matches <- bind_rows(
  best_topic_match(terms_a, terms_b) |>
    mutate(comparison = "seed 42 vs 7", .before = 1),
  best_topic_match(terms_a, terms_c) |>
    mutate(comparison = "seed 42 vs 2024", .before = 1),
  best_topic_match(terms_b, terms_c) |>
    mutate(comparison = "seed 7 vs 2024", .before = 1)
)

seed_summary <- seed_matches |>
  summarise(
    mean_shared_terms = round(mean(shared_top_10_terms), 2),
    minimum_shared_terms = min(shared_top_10_terms),
    maximum_shared_terms = max(shared_top_10_terms),
    total_shared_terms = sum(shared_top_10_terms),
    .by = comparison
  )

within_fit_overlap <- expand_grid(
  topic_first = sort(unique(terms_a$topic)),
  topic_second = sort(unique(terms_a$topic))
) |>
  filter(topic_first < topic_second) |>
  mutate(
    shared_top_10_terms = map2_int(
      topic_first,
      topic_second,
      \(first_topic, second_topic) {
        length(intersect(
          terms_a$term[terms_a$topic == first_topic],
          terms_a$term[terms_a$topic == second_topic]
        ))
      }
    )
  )
within_fit_mean <- mean(within_fit_overlap$shared_top_10_terms)

seed_null <- permutation_null(
  observed = mean(seed_matches$shared_top_10_terms[seed_matches$comparison == "seed 42 vs 7"]),
  replicate_fn = function() {
    shuffled_terms <- terms_b |>
      mutate(topic = sample(topic, n(), replace = FALSE))

    mean(best_topic_match(terms_a, shuffled_terms)$shared_top_10_terms)
  },
  replicates = 500L,
  seed = 5502L,
  alternative = "greater"
)

seed_null_display <- seed_null |>
  mutate(across(c(observed, null_mean, null_low, null_high, p_value), \(x) round(x, 3)))
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(
  seed_matches,
  col.names = c("Comparison", "Topic in first run", "Matched topic in second run", "Shared top-10 terms"),
  caption = "Best-matched topic overlaps across three five-topic runs",
  row.names = FALSE
)

knitr::kable(
  seed_summary,
  col.names = c("Comparison", "Mean shared top-10 terms", "Minimum", "Maximum", "Total shared terms"),
  caption = "Topic overlap after matching arbitrary topic numbers",
  row.names = FALSE
)

knitr::kable(
  seed_null_display,
  col.names = c("Observed", "Null mean", "Null low", "Null high", "p-value", "Replicates", "Alternative"),
  caption = "Frequency-preserving allocation null for seed 42 vs seed 7 overlap",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  identical(seed_summary$mean_shared_terms, c(5.6, 5.4, 5.0)),
  identical(seed_summary$minimum_shared_terms, c(4L, 4L, 3L)),
  identical(seed_summary$maximum_shared_terms, c(7L, 7L, 6L)),
  identical(seed_summary$total_shared_terms, c(28L, 27L, 25L)),
  identical(as.numeric(within_fit_mean), 3.9),
  identical(as.numeric(seed_null_display$observed), 5.6),
  identical(as.numeric(seed_null_display$null_mean), 4.901),
  identical(as.numeric(seed_null_display$p_value), 0.03)
)
```

The three full-corpus five-topic fits show modest repeatability. Matched topics
share 5.6, 5.4, and 5.0 of their top 10 terms on average across the three
pairwise comparisons. Distinct topics within the seed-42 fit already share
`r round(within_fit_mean, 1)` terms on average.

The null keeps the same 50 top-term rows, which contain repeated high-frequency
terms. It randomly allocates those rows across five equal-sized topics. Its mean is
`r round(seed_null$null_mean, 3)`, compared with observed overlap
`r round(seed_null$observed, 1)` and p =
`r round(seed_null$p_value, 3)`. This is limited evidence of repeatability for
these three `k = 5` fits. It does not establish that five topics are more
stable than another topic count.

## Changing k changes the question

A four-topic fit provides a sensitivity check rather than the same model as a five-topic fit. After `k` changes, topic numbers no longer identify corresponding topics across models.

```{r}
set.seed(42)
lda_4 <- LDA(
  lda_input,
  k = 4,
  method = "VEM",
  control = list(seed = 42)
)

topics_4 <- top_terms(lda_4, n = 8L) |>
  summarise(
    top_terms = paste(term, collapse = ", "),
    top_term = first(term),
    .by = topic
  )

shared_first_terms <- length(intersect(topics_a$top_terms |> str_extract("^[^,]+"), topics_4$top_term))
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(
  topics_4 |>
    select(topic, top_terms),
  col.names = c("Topic number", "Top terms"),
  caption = "Top terms from a four-topic LDA model with seed 42",
  row.names = FALSE
)

knitr::kable(
  tibble(shared_first_terms = shared_first_terms),
  col.names = "Shared first terms with the seed-42 five-topic fit",
  caption = "A small comparison after changing k",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  identical(nrow(topics_4), 4L),
  identical(
    topics_4$top_term,
    c("must", "people", "government", "public")
  ),
  identical(shared_first_terms, 2L),
  identical(topics_4$top_terms[1], "must, government, people, can, us, power, country, now")
)
```

The first terms for the four-topic model are `must`, `people`, `government`, and `public`. Two are also first terms in the five-topic seed-42 fit. This count does not give an estimate of stability because a different `k` specifies a different modeling target.

## What to remember

- LDA groups words that co-occur across paragraph documents.
- This lesson used 1,377 paragraph documents and 2,587 features.
- No diagnostic supplies a single correct `k`. The choice depends on the
  intended resolution and purpose.
- Perplexity, coherence, and exclusivity can favor different topic counts.
- Three full-corpus `k = 5` fits showed modest repeatability. That check did not
  compare topic counts.
- VEM and Gibbs sampling fit LDA through different algorithms. Other topic-model
  families answer different questions.
- A different `k` requires new topic labels.
- A topic name is a reading aid, not a finding produced by the model.

Keep the topic numbers with their model settings. Reassess the interpretation after model settings change.
